item.description: Reddit will start testing a logged-in-only experience in select non-US markets in Q4. The company's CEO says the login requirement will help Reddit retain new users. It will also provide more signals for ads targeting and help protect access to the site's data. The changes will make it significantly easier for Reddit to understand who uses Reddit and why, which will help the site manage things like AI scraping and evolving search habits.

It is currently waiting on regulatory approval before it can be sold to customers. It has already received Breakthrough Device Designation from the US FDA, which will help speed review of the device.

item.title: A golden age of science is coming (16 minute read)
item.description: Progress has started to accelerate in science in the last two years. AI can send hordes of superhumanly fast, well-read, and mathematically gifted researchers to accelerate scientific research. It is possible AI will enable new types of discovery and ways of understanding the natural world that no network of humans would ever be able to discover. Unless humans have actually somehow discovered most of the actual exploitable regularities in the Universe, we're about to enter a new golden age of science.

item.title: A Little Determinism (16 minute read)
item.description: Adding constraints to AI agents usually makes them less capable. Sometimes the solution is to create a template or a complete multi-stage workflow. The challenge is in creating the deterministic behavior while retaining the agent's freedom to use the best tools for the job. This post discusses a solution that uses a man-in-the-middle egress proxy that forces behavior by denying actions and forces reactions via automated messages.

item.title: Making agents fast - what I've learnt over the last 12 months (12 minute read)
item.description: Knowing what part of inference a project relies on for speed is important. Check thinking budgets, and read traces, as they often contain valuable insight into what an agent wants to do. Give agents the tools they want rather than what you think they need. Faster hardware still matters, sandboxing and microVMs add complexity, parallelization helps, and classic software performance optimization is still relevant.

item.title: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist (5 minute read)

Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle moved quickly to freeze some of the stolen assets. The heist appears to have been conducted by a North Korean hacking group. Binance's founder said in a post on social media that users' funds are safe.

item.description: Apeiron, a Delta-class suborbital spacecraft from Virgin Galactic, is being moved from Virgin Galactic's Spaceship Factory in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico. After its arrival, aircraft engineers and technicians will complete work on the vehicle's avionics equipment and flight software. Apeiron will still require several ground tests and test flights before it can make a free flight. Virgin Galactic expects Apeiron's first commercial spaceflight to take place early in the second quarter of 2027.

item.title: Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen (3 minute read)
item.description: The Grid is a factory-scale robot that can build circuit boards on demand. Every board takes its own route through the factory, which has machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder, and inspect. With The Grid, printing one unit of 100 designs is as easy as printing 100 units of one, and prototypes and production batches run on the same machines. It allows companies to manufacture huge numbers of low-volume boards, and could help bring manufacturing back to the US.

item.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software (13 minute read)
item.description: Researchers based in China have collaborated to create a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with specified functions. This could enable anyone to design proteins - if they have a lab that can sort the good designs from the failures. The model's success rate is not great, but it can still get the job done. The tool likely won't remove the need for biologists, but it could help accelerate research.

item.title: Sunlight at night: US startup's demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticism (6 minute read)
item.description: Reflect Orbital is a US-based startup that plans to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight onto the Earth during night-time. The Federal Communications Commission has approved the startup's proposal to launch an initial demonstration satellite next year. The test will reflect sunlight in 3-mile-wide beams in strengths from moonlight up to the brightness of the Sun at noon. While the technology could be helpful for search-and-rescue operations, among other applications, critics say that it threatens a harmful change to the separation of night and day, with a huge number of unresolved questions and significant potential impacts.

item.title: The Biggest Takeaways From Anthropic's IPO Prospectus (8 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic unveiled its IPO paperwork yesterday, putting it on track to go public as soon as the week before Thanksgiving. The 400-page prospectus tells a story of how the company could usher in a new era of progress that will transform how people code, conduct research, build financial models, and automate routine tasks. It also warned that AI could lead to the development of new bioweapons, destabilize the geopolitical order, and evolve beyond the ability of humans to understand and control. Anthropic plans to trade on the NASDAQ under the ticker 'ANT', with a valuation expected to land between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

item.title: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding (12 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI has announced three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics. For the math result, which is about harmonic analysis, the AI lab will release the AI output, so researchers are free to organize their own efforts to explain the result. OpenAI will form an external group of collaborators to explain the computer science result, which is about complexity theory, and will make the AI output publicly available. The lab will also form an external group of collaborators for the physics result, which is about quantum field theory, but defer to them on the release of the materials.

item.title: 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear (9 minute read)
item.description: Solar power will likely provide 10% of the world's power by the end of the year. Solar electricity is the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history as it has become unbelievably cheap. China is still the world's biggest solar power producer by far, but the installations in the US are skyrocketing. Even with tariffs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US, and it is getting built regardless of political lines.

item.title: The Counting House (49 minute read)
item.description: The Counting House pattern adds AI to systems that handle large volumes of human work, notably customer service departments. It can be used to control and improve costs, quality, and human ramp-up time using comparatively cheap AI models. A Counting House uses classic data science and engineering to put lower-tier models on hardened rails to support human workflows. It allows teams to measure and report how well models do against their human counterparts.

item.title: How the Claude Code team does code review (18 minute read)
item.description: Claude writes about 90% of the code in Claude Code. This post explains how the team reviews the code at the volume its agents produce. The team moved most of the reading in the review stage to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. This resulted in merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubling while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40% between June and September.

item.title: Microsoft Will Offer Buyouts to 60,000 Employees (3 minute read)

The voluntary retirement program is part of a broader shift by Microsoft to alter its performance system and how it awards bonuses and stock options.

item.title: The End of the Internet (18 minute read)
item.description: Blogging began to die when Google started aggregating the internet. Social media made it much easier to create and share content, but this caused the amount of content to increase by orders of magnitude. Algorithms started to matter, and then these sites started becoming personal entertainment sites, tuned for engagement. The latest series of security vulnerabilities unveiled by AI will further shrink the public internet.

item.title: Jane Street and Rivals Are Now Fighting for AI Power as Well as Pace (17 minute read)
item.description: High-frequency traders are now racing for compute. They are investing in the sector as it secures them access to greater processing capacity and faster chips. As they increasingly rely on machine learning, their success is directly tied to their computing power. While the risks are significant, most high-speed traders see few options if they want to avoid becoming obsolete.

item.title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions (7 minute read)
item.description: Researchers have developed an implantable neural chip that tracks communication across brain regions. It can record brain activity and extract biomarkers that describe the strength of brain waves and synchrony between signals from different brain regions. These signals can be decoded using a machine-learning algorithm to distinguish between cognitive and emotional states. The capability to extract brain-network biomarkers to trigger precisely timed stimulation has many applications across next-generation neurotechnology.

item.title: US military gives Elon Musk's SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data (7 minute read)
item.description: SpaceX has been granted access to restricted space tracking data by the US military. The access raises new national security questions as well as questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth's orbit to a donor. Elon Musk's Doge program fired many of the federal government's space traffic control staff in 2025, and the administration has twice attempted to financially gut the Traffic Coordination System for Space department. The moves have been widely viewed in the industry as an attempt by Musk to privatize space traffic control.

item.title: The Factory in Phoenix That Could Save American Manufacturing (28 minute read)
item.description: TSMC Arizona's first plant has been producing chips for two years. Its rate of output in Phoenix is comparable to that in Taiwan. This article looks at the impact the factory had on Phoenix, the employees who moved to America to work there, and the chip manufacturing industry in the US.

item.title: The Signal Chats That Cost OpenAI Researchers Their Jobs (13 minute read)
item.description: Three OpenAI safety researchers were fired after security officers discovered Signal chats with disappearing messages turned on on their personal devices. OpenAI claimed the researchers were fired for violating clear policies for handling sensitive information and not for raising safety concerns or speaking out. The researchers had spent recent months at the company pushing for more industry collaboration on safety. They claim their firings will serve as an excuse for OpenAI to close a channel to independent third-party insight.

item.title: Amazon's New Tablet Is a Credible iPad Rival for Much Less Money (11 minute read)
item.description: The Alexa Tablet lineup offers a more open approach to software than Amazon's previous Fire brand that lets consumers use the devices like any other Android tablet. Users can download apps from the Google Play Store and access popular services like Gmail and YouTube. Amazon previously restricted access to its own app marketplace. The 12-inch Alexa Tablet Pro is well constructed and has a smooth 12-hertz display, making it competitive with Apple's iPads.

item.title: SpaceX in Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites for New Network (4 minute read)
item.description: SpaceX is in talks with Crown Castle Inc., one of the largest owners of cellular towers in the US, as part of its plans to secure a minimum of 80,000 cell sites across the country. Crown Castle is likely also in talks with Amazon and other satellite-based telecom providers regarding leasing deals. Elon Musk has openly discussed creating a standalone wireless carrier from scratch. SpaceX recently acquired low-band spectrum and has received approval to launch 15,000 satellites to provide mobile service directly to phones.

item.title: Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42% (3 minute read)
item.description: Moderna and Merck's personalized mRNA vaccines against melanoma demonstrate how mRNA technology has the potential to fundamentally challenge how cancer is treated. The vaccine's success offers a new paradigm for cancer therapies. The companies are already engaging with regulatory authorities to get the vaccine approved.

item.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale (23 minute read)
item.description: We need ways to prove that code is free from bugs. Formal software verification, which could provide this guarantee, has always required years of expert effort, but LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale. This enables new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Formal verification will likely become an essential part of secure software development as model capabilities continue to improve.

item.title: Anthropic builds its own source control system (15 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic employs around 3,500 staff, but its coding output is closer to that of a company with 35,000 to 70,000 staff. Big tech companies like Google and Meta moved off Git a long time ago because it did not scale for them. Both built their own custom solutions, just like Anthropic did with Scion. This post provides some details about how Anthropic's custom source control system works.

item.title: An artist's take on AI in math (9 minute read)
item.description: Mathematics seems to be a field where the outputs are celebrated less as examples of subjective expression and more as advancements in knowledge and understanding. A mathematician's work may be informed by their experience, but that's not what gives their contributions value. Mathematical knowledge remains objectively true whether it is observed by humans or sea sponges or computer programs.

item.title: ‘If Anything Happens to This Guy … Everyone Is Screwed' (13 minute read)
item.description: Ondřej Surý is one of the volunteers who helps maintain and automate patches for PHP. He alone is responsible for most of the world's distribution of PHP. His work, along with just a handful of others, has allowed countless websites and organizations to fix the recently revealed PHP vulnerabilities quickly. He's become arguably the unsung hero of the entire internet, despite the fact that the only compensation he receives for his work is from donations. This article features an interview with Surý where he discusses the unfolding AI-cybersecurity crisis, how the internet's infrastructure is maintained by small crews of volunteers, and how it feels to save the web.

item.title: Anthropic Joins the AI Agent Race With Claude Duet (3 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic's Claude Duet joins a fast-growing field of AI assistants that take actions and perform tasks on their own. Unlike OpenAI's dots and Meta's Muse, Anthropic's agent was built for work and is less capable at personal errands. It can connect to more than 6,000 outside apps and make purchases through Link, Stripe's digital wallet, and Shopify's Shop Pay. The agent shows users exactly what it plans to do before performing actions, and some actions, like trading stocks or moving money between accounts, are blocked even with user approval. The wait list to use the agent is now open to Anthropic's Pro and Max plan subscribers.

item.title: Musk Tries to Lock In His Tesla-SpaceX Dream Before Trump's Exit (11 minute read)
item.description: Elon Musk is fully behind a combination of SpaceX and Tesla, his two most valuable companies. He is pushing to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so it closes during the Trump administration. The timing will depend on when Tesla's board gets comfortable with the details - SpaceX shareholder approval is less of an obstacle, as Musk controls more than 80% of the voting power. Combining the companies before the end of this administration would consolidate Musk's corporate power before a potentially less accommodating political and financial environment takes hold.

item.title: Tesla starts Optimus robot production in California as profit falls 43% (3 minute read)
item.description: Tesla has started production of its Optimus humanoid robot at its factory in Fremont, California. While the company admits there is still more work to be done before the robot is fully safe and reliable, it says it has proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product. Elon Musk says Tesla will be able to make 20,000 units per week by the end of 2027. Tesla's profits fell 43% in the third quarter due to heavy investments in its Optimus robots, AI, and autonomous driving.

item.title: Physicists trap and tame single particle of antimatter for months (12 minute read)
item.description: Physicists at Northwestern University have coaxed a single positron (the antimatter counterpart of an electron) into an exquisitely controlled quantum state for the first time. The scientists cooled the fast-moving particle to nearly absolute zero after capturing it from radioactive decay, and then suspended it in a near-perfect vacuum, resulting in a state where the positron behaved much like an artificial atom with quantum energy levels scientists can precisely control and observe. The technique could enable the most precise test yet of a fundamental symmetry between electrons and their antimatter counterparts.

item.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure (11 minute read)
item.description: Git traffic grew exponentially over the past year. During that time, GitHub started moving almost all of its repositories to Azure. This post discusses how per-reference quorums will bring over the rest, and how object storage lets reads scale independently.

item.title: The Topology of an LLM Agent Loop With Tool Use (7 minute read)
item.description: An agent is three things: a model, an agentic loop, and a set of tools. Where these run has implications for cost, capability, effectiveness, and security. If you focus on topology, you can break down any agentic product and reason about what a product can and cannot do. There isn't one perfect loop - good UX for a general-purpose chatbot is not the same as good UX for a coding agent.

item.title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day (2 minute read)
item.description: AI has discovered critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, prompting the US National Security Agency to advise organizations using PHP to either update immediately or take their systems offline until they can. Node.js has released an update that fixes four high-severity vulnerabilities. LiteLLM was compromised by an attacker who injected malicious code. eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority, had its private keys compromised, potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. These unrelated issues highlight the challenges cybersecurity teams now face.

item.title: How Mark Zuckerberg Pushed Meta to Shield Him From California's Proposed Wealth Tax (6 minute read)
item.description: California's proposed tax on billionaires prompted Mark Zuckerberg to leverage the board at Meta to get the company to protect him from it. He issued an ultimatum to the board on September 9 that he would sell his home in Palo Alto, and the listing would be public, if a deal wasn't struck by September 13. The board decided to issue a new class of stock to shareholders that Zuckerberg could sell to pay the potential wealth tax without cutting into his 60.6% voting power. California's proposal would assess a one-time 5% tax on all holdings of billionaires who lived in California as of January 1, 2026.

item.title: Tesla and SpaceX Formed Committees to Discuss Potential Merger, Elon Musk Says (6 minute read)
item.description: SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. While Elon Musk thinks there's a lot of merit in combining the companies, the special committees have yet to reach an agreement, and there's no guarantee that they will. Musk is not on either committee. Shareholders will get to vote on the matter. A deal this large will attract regulatory scrutiny.

item.title: Anthropic S-1 Shows Red-Hot Growth, Risks, and Massive Computing Costs (8 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic's draft initial public offering prospectus recorded a net loss of more than $80 billion in the first half of this year. It also lays out a long list of risk factors that include uncertainty over how the company plans to prevent its AI models from causing harm and protect itself from those liabilities. Anthropic is generating breakneck revenue growth, but it faces challenges such as uncertain access to compute. It has signaled that it could potentially spend $750 billion in the next few years on obtaining more compute capacity.

item.title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins (16 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic asked an internal research model to design mini binders, small proteins that attach tightly to a target, against scorpion neurotoxins as part of its work in experimenting with how Claude can accelerate drug discovery. 17 of the 211 designs tested met Anthropic's criteria. Anthropic has not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so it is not claiming to have produced an antivenom. However, the study is a promising first step towards using AI to design credible binders against hard-to-target toxins in days, with lab confirmation within weeks. The challenge, as always, will be turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs.

item.title: I Paid $60 for Two Humanoids to Clean My Home In San Francisco (8 minute read)
item.description: You can now pay for human operator-controlled robots to clean your house in San Francisco. This post describes the experience of hiring Tau Robotics' robots to clean a home for an hour. It details what the experience is like, examines the economics for the user and for the company, and tries to predict what a future with humanoids and advanced robots doing productive work would look like.

item.title: Increase your slope (22 minute read)
item.description: Become an expert at something small, take ownership of the problems around you, and get comfortable with having opinions. These things build on each other, and new employees can start doing all of them much sooner than they think. Practiced over time, workers will find themselves answering questions they used to ask, making decisions they used to need help with, and taking on problems they wouldn't have known how to approach.

item.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals (23 minute read)
item.description: Decision models are an appealing alternative to LLM judges for automated evals. However, whether they're the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of the use case. Many people leave the default decision threshold at 0.50 without checking whether that's appropriate for the task, leaving a lot of performance on the table. This post shows how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models, compares cost and performance between models, and explores how to interpret model scores and how calibration can make them more useful.

item.title: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) (7 minute read)
item.description: AI's gains have been so large that how we work with it has to change. Before, the work was divided between AI and humans. Now, humans summon agents when needed, assign them work, and evaluate what comes back. While it is the most powerful way to use AI, it carries new risks as we lose control over what AI is doing to get those results.
